survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The report uses OECD PISA and OECD PIAAC microdata to compare literacy/reading and numeracy/mathematics proficiency across pseudo-cohorts (age 15 in PISA and age ~24–27 in PIAAC). Both PISA and PIAAC are complex, multi-stage survey designs (PISA: two-stage school then student sampling; PIAAC: household-based sampling with interviewer-administered background questionnaire and direct assessment). The report discusses that PISA results are based on representative samples of in-school 15-year-olds and that PIAAC targets non-institutionalised adults aged 16–65, implying that analysts should use the official sampling weights when estimating population-representative means and gaps. The manuscript does not provide enough detail to confirm whether the authors applied specific weight variables (e.g., PISA student weights or PIAAC weights) in their computations; therefore, weight-aware replication guidance should follow the official PISA/PIAAC technical standards for the relevant cycles and countries.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The report relies on PISA and PIAAC proficiency scales derived from IRT and plausible values (PISA draws five PVs per domain up to 2012; PIAAC draws ten PVs). However, it does not document a specific missing-data strategy for the analytic comparisons (e.g., whether cases with missing background variables were excluded or whether missing background items were imputed). This is a reporting gap because missingness handling can affect subgroup gap estimates, especially when restricting to pseudo-cohort age bands and excluding certain countries or migration cases.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The core analyses use pseudo-cohort comparisons between PISA 2000 (age 15) and PIAAC 2011/12 (age ~26–28) for the same birth-cohort, with additional comparisons using PISA 2003 matched to PIAAC age 26–28 (and for numeracy, also PISA 2003 matched to PIAAC 23–25). The report excludes PIAAC respondents who report being born outside the country and who do not provide migration timing, while including foreign-born individuals who migrated prior to age 10 (age-10 threshold chosen to ensure they would have been in the PISA target population at age 15 and had adequate language proficiency). It also excludes England, the Netherlands, Northern Ireland (UK) and the Russian Federation from the main pseudo-cohort analyses due to response-rate/coverage issues (UK and Netherlands PISA 2000/2003 response rates below standards; Russian Federation PIAAC excludes Moscow municipal area). For PIAAC age-band precision, the PIAAC age band is widened to 26–28 (and for some numeracy analyses, 23–25) because the target PIAAC sample size is insufficient for single birth-cohort estimates. In the Poland linking experiment, the PISA grade-10 national option includes students aged 16+; students aged 18+ are excluded from linking due to selection concerns, and PISA is restricted to ages 15+ while PIAAC is not restricted by upper age bound.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report compares literacy/reading and numeracy/mathematics proficiency across pseudo-cohorts by linking PISA (age 15) and PIAAC (young adulthood, ~24–27) for countries participating in both assessments. Because PISA and PIAAC were not designed to be psychometrically linked, the report does not estimate growth by directly comparing raw scores; instead it computes standardised performance gaps using a modified Cohen’s d across subgroups defined consistently in both studies (gender, parental education, and home resources proxied by number of books). The report finds that socio-economic disparities in literacy and numeracy generally persist and often widen from age 15 to young adulthood, especially at the bottom of the performance distribution, while gender gaps in literacy show strong convergence by age ~27 and numeracy gender gaps remain small but widen somewhat. It also provides a feasibility “proof of concept” for linking in Poland using statistical matching and concordance, highlighting that lack of an established PISA–PIAAC link limits precision and interpretability of growth claims. Limitations include the pseudo-cohort design (no true individual longitudinal tracking), exclusion rules and small subgroup samples in PIAAC, and the inability to establish causality from the observational comparisons.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD technical report-style synthesis and framework comparison rather than an empirical machine-learning prediction study. It does not train or evaluate ML models, and it does not report predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) for a supervised learner, so main_findings and ml_techniques are intentionally empty. Sample sizes and per-country Ns are not provided for the full pseudo-cohort analyses in the extracted text, and the report focuses on assessment comparability, subgroup gap patterns, and a statistical linking feasibility exercise rather than a single unified analytic dataset with a documented ML pipeline.
